title: Sequence of Returns Risk: Why the Order of Your Retirement Returns Matters More Than the Average
metaDescription: Two retirees can earn the same average return and end up with very different retirement outcomes. Here's why timing matters more than averages.
bodyHtml:
Imagine two retirees. Both start with $500,000. Both withdraw the same amount every year. Both earn the exact same average annual return over a 30-year retirement. One of them runs out of money 8 years early. The other dies with more than they started with.

The difference isn't luck, and it isn't fees. It's the order the returns showed up in. That's called sequence of returns risk, and it's one of the least understood risks in retirement planning.

What Sequence of Returns Risk Actually Is

Sequence of returns risk, also known as sequence risk or SORR, is the danger that poor investment returns early in retirement, combined with ongoing withdrawals, will significantly reduce a portfolio's value and limit its ability to recover. The math works fine as long as you're only adding money to your accounts. It gets dangerous the moment you start pulling money out.

Once portfolio withdrawals begin, investment returns become path-dependent, meaning the order of gains and losses matters. A market decline early in retirement can have a much greater effect than the same decline happening later, because you're selling shares at depressed prices just to pay your bills — locking in losses that a growing portfolio would never have to realize.

Why the First Decade Matters Most

This is especially the case in the first decade of retirement, when portfolio balances are largest and most vulnerable to market downturns. Some planners call this stretch — the last few years before retirement through the first several years after — the "retirement red zone," because it includes the years before and after retirement, when market declines can have a larger effect on future income.

Here's the part that trips people up: average annual returns do not show how the timing of gains and losses affects retirees who are making regular portfolio withdrawals. A portfolio can average a perfectly respectable 6% a year for three decades and still fail, if the bad years land right at the start.

A Simple Example

Say two retirees each start with $500,000, withdraw $30,000 at the start of each year, and experience the exact same five annual returns — just in opposite order. Retiree A gets the bad year first; Retiree B gets it last.

YearRetiree A: ReturnRetiree A: BalanceRetiree B: ReturnRetiree B: Balance
1-20%$376,000+20%$564,000
2+5%$363,300+15%$614,100
3+10%$366,630+10%$642,510
4+15%$387,125+5%$643,136
5+20%$428,549-20%$490,508

Same five returns. Same average (6%). Same withdrawals. Retiree B ends up with roughly $62,000 more than Retiree A after just five years — a gap that only widens as the withdrawals continue. The only difference was which year the -20% landed in.

You Can't Just "Wait It Out"

During your working years, a market crash is annoying but survivable — you keep contributing, keep buying shares at lower prices, and the market eventually recovers. Retirement flips that. Market downturns can have a much more significant impact on your portfolio and your lifetime income strategy, because you don't have the luxury of time for your investments to recover. You're not buying the dip. You're selling into it to cover rent and groceries.

How to Actually Reduce This Risk

You can't control what the market does the year you retire. But you can control how exposed you are to it. A few approaches that actually move the needle:

  • Keep a cash buffer. Holding one to two years of living expenses in cash or short-term bonds means you're not forced to sell stocks during a downturn — you draw from cash instead and let the portfolio recover.
  • Use a bucket strategy. Split your money into short-term (cash), medium-term (bonds), and long-term (stocks) buckets so you're always spending from the safest bucket first.
  • Build in flexible withdrawals. Rigid, fixed withdrawal amounts make sequence risk worse. A plan that trims spending in down years — even modestly — extends how long the portfolio lasts.
  • Adjust your equity allocation before you retire. Dialing back stock exposure in the 5 years before retirement (and the first few years after) shrinks how much a crash can cost you, exactly during the window when it would hurt most.
  • Delay retirement or work part-time if the market drops right before you planned to stop. Even one or two extra years of income, or a part-time bridge job, can meaningfully reduce how hard your portfolio has to work.

Where This Fits With the 4% Rule

The 4% rule gives you a starting withdrawal rate based on historical worst-case sequences — it's already built with sequence risk in mind. But it's a guideline, not a guarantee. If you retire directly into a bad sequence, sticking rigidly to a fixed withdrawal amount without adjusting can accelerate exactly the problem this article is describing. Treat your withdrawal rate as a starting point you're willing to flex, not a number carved in stone.

Why This Matters Even If Retirement Is Decades Away

Sequence risk isn't just a retiree problem — it's a planning problem. If you're still accumulating, this is one more reason your asset allocation should get more conservative as you approach retirement, not after you've already gotten there. The five years on either side of your retirement date are the ones that matter most; that's not the time to find out your portfolio is more aggressive than you thought. If you want a quick gut-check on how exposed your current mix is, running your numbers through a tool like Grade My Finance can show you where your allocation and withdrawal plans actually stand before a bad sequence forces the question.

The Bottom Line

Two people can do everything else right — save diligently, invest reasonably, retire with the same balance — and still end up in very different places because of when they retired, not how they invested.
